narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward a more favorable outcome. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not strong enough to overcome the much larger negative effects from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 28, also well below the accepted average of 37, added further concern, though it carried less weight than your school performance. Your middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class standing in the remaining years and consider retaking the LSAT to bring your score closer to the typical range of successful applicants. Stronger performance in these areas can meaningfully change future predictions. (248 words)
